title: Geminate roots and other irregular verbs

objectives.can: Recognise forms of roots whose second and third consonants are alike, and of doubly weak verbs.

explanation.summary: Two last kinds of Hebrew verb remain. Geminate roots have a second and third consonant that are alike, and the verb often contracts them into one. Doubly weak verbs are weak in two places at once, so their forms can shrink to a single visible consonant. This lesson also gathers the method for finding a root from any form.

sections.heading: Geminate roots: two like consonants
body: A geminate root has a second and a third consonant that are the same letter. סָבַב, 'turn, go around', is ס ב ב. תָּמַם, 'be complete', is ת מ ם. Because the two alike letters stand side by side, the verb can contract them into one doubled letter, and the form then looks as if it had only two root consonants.

Look at the Qal of תָּמַם. The 3rd masculine singular qatal is תַּם, 'it was finished', with a single closed syllable. The 3rd plural is תַּמּוּ, in which the מ is doubled by a dagesh before the ending -וּ. The yiqtol is יִתַּמּוּ, the infinitive construct is תֹּם. The doubled letter is the sign that two like consonants have merged.

In the prefix conjugations a geminate Qal is often built with a prefix vowel and an o-vowel in the stem. For סָבַב, 'go around', the yiqtol is found as יָסֹב (with ָ under the prefix) and as יִסֹּב (with the first root consonant doubled). The wayyiqtol is וַיִּסֹּב in the singular and וַיָּסֹבּוּ in the plural. The imperative is סֹב, 'turn!'.
The Hiphil of a geminate often shows the old doubling again: וַיַּסֵּב in Joshua 6:11 is the Hiphil wayyiqtol, 'and he caused to go around'; the Hiphil qatal is הֵסֵב.

sections.heading: Geminates that keep their consonants apart
body: The contraction is not universal. A few forms keep all three consonants, for example the qatal וְסָבַב, or the participle סוֹבֵב. Stative geminates such as שָׁמֵם, 'be desolate', often show their two like consonants separately in the qatal (שָׁמְמוּ) and in the participle (שֹׁמֵם).

Some forms can be taken for another class. וַיֵּרַע, from רָעַע 'be evil, bad', has a prefix vowel ֵ and no sign of a doubled letter; it might at first remind you of a first-yod or a hollow verb. This is why the method below counts the consonants and tests the classes in an order: a geminate is recognised by a doubled letter, by a missing third consonant, or by a short stem with an o-vowel.

The root חָנַן, 'be gracious', is common in prayers: the imperative with a suffix is חָנֵּנִי, 'be gracious to me'. The root מָדַד, 'measure', has the wayyiqtol וַיָּמָד in the singular (with ָ in the stem) and וַיָּמֹדּוּ in the plural.

sections.heading: Doubly weak verbs
body: Some verbs are weak in two positions at once, and each weakness applies its own rule. נָטָה, 'stretch out', has a first נ that can drop out and a last ה that is cut off in the shortened forms. The wayyiqtol is therefore וַיֵּט, 'and he stretched out', where after the prefix only one root consonant remains: ט. The imperative נְטֵה keeps the נ and loses nothing but the vowel letter.

נָכָה, 'strike', is in the same pattern. Its common Hiphil wayyiqtol is וַיַּךְ, 'and he struck', in which the first נ has been absorbed and the last ה has gone, leaving only the ך. יָרָה, 'throw, shoot', is a first-yod and third-he verb. Its Hiphil wayyiqtol is וַיּוֹר, 'and he shot', with just י and ר showing.

Verbs with a final א belong here too when they have another weakness: נָשָׂא, 'lift', has a first נ that drops (וַיִּשָּׂא); בּוֹא, 'come', is hollow and ends in א (וַיָּבֹא); יָצָא, 'go out', begins with a root י and ends in א (וַיֵּצֵא); and רָאָה, 'see', has a middle א and a final ה, which is why its short wayyiqtol is as small as וַיַּרְא.

sections.heading: A method for finding the root
body: Almost any form of any verb can be traced to a headword by the same few steps. First, strip what is added to the root: the וְ or וַ in front, any preposition or article, any suffix. Second, take off the person prefix (י, ת, א, נ) or the ending (-וּ, -תִּי, -נוּ and the rest). Third, count the consonants that are left. Fourth, test the classes in the order the table suggests.

Three consonants left usually means a regular verb or a verb with a guttural. Two consonants left means a letter has dropped out: the third (a third-he verb), the first (first-nun or first-yod/waw), the middle (a hollow verb), or a doubled letter has merged two (a geminate). One consonant left means two weaknesses at once. At each step, check the headword in a lexicon and let the meaning in the verse confirm it, because more than one class may fit the same letters.

misunderstandings: A doubled letter in the middle of a form does not always mean a geminate root. A dagesh can also come from an assimilated first נ (וַיִּפֹּל) or from the Piel stem. Count what is left after the prefix and decide with the headword.
A geminate root has three consonants, not two. Contracted forms such as תַּם look as if they had two, but the lexicon lists the root as תָּמַם.
Doubly weak verbs are not random. Each of the two weaknesses follows its own rule, and the form is what is left when both rules have been applied.
One form can sometimes belong to two roots. Check the lexicon and the context before you decide: the same three letters may be a geminate in one verse and a different class in another.

deeper.heading: The word geminate
body: The grammarians' word comes from the Latin for 'twin'. Older Hebrew grammars also call them 'ayin-ayin' roots, after the position of the repeated letter in the model root used to name positions. What matters in reading is that the pair of like consonants either merges into one doubled letter or stays apart, and the two cases follow different patterns.

quoted.english: And the second day they compassed the city once, and returned into the camp; so they did six days.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Three verbs from three classes in one verse. וַיָּסֹבּוּ is the Qal wayyiqtol 3rd plural of the geminate סָבַב: 'and they went around'; the ב is doubled before the ending. וַיָּשֻׁבוּ is from the hollow root שׁוּב, 'return'. עָשׂוּ is the third-he qatal 3rd plural of עָשָׂה, 'they did'. Telling these apart is the method of this lesson.

check.prompt: A form shows a prefix וַיֵּ and then a single ט. What is the best first guess about its root?
options: A geminate whose two like letters merged
A doubly weak verb in which two root letters have dropped out
check.explain: One consonant left after the prefix means two root letters are missing, which points to a doubly weak verb. A regular verb shows three consonants, and a geminate leaves two, one doubled.

reading.why: The ark is carried around Jericho. The passage uses the geminate סָבַב in the Qal and the Hiphil (וַיַּסֵּב, וַיָּסֹבּוּ) beside the hollow, doubly weak and third-he verbs that this unit has just taught.
